nodes.name: Apply inversion rule
nodes.statement: By the inversion rule (\ref{eq4}) the elements \ $\tilde{x}_{i}$\ of the ball $\tilde I_{i}$\ now connect to an $x_{i}\in C$ \ given by \begin{equation} x_{i}=3^{-n} \cdot 3^{-n(- \cdot i2^{-r})}\times b_i, \ b_i=\Sigma \text{ }b_{ij}\text{ }3^{-j}, \text{ }b_{ij}\in \{0,2\} \end{equation} \noindent where $\lambda =a_i\times b_i \in (0,1).$
nodes.statement_short: The inversion rule connects x~_i to a point x_i of C, eq. (11).
nodes.section: 3.1 Middle Third Cantor Set: An Example

nodes.name: Primary and secondary scales
nodes.statement: (Infinitesimal) Scales $\epsilon _{n}=3^{-n},$\ \ are the \emph{primary} scales when the scales $3^{-k_{i}}$(or equivalently $2^{-r}$) are the {\em secondary} scales.
nodes.statement_short: Name 3^{-n} primary and 2^{-r} secondary scales.
nodes.section: 3.1 Middle Third Cantor Set: An Example

nodes.name: Multiplicative identity
nodes.statement: Finally, to verify the new multiplicative representation one notes that there exists $y_{i}\in C$ in a neighbourhood of $x_{i}$ so that \bigskip \begin{center} $y_{i}=3^{-n}$ $c_{i},$ $\ \ c_{i}=$ $\Sigma $\ $c_{ij}$ $3^{-j},$ \ $ c_{ij}\in \{0,2\}$\ \end{center} \noindent and \begin{equation} x_{i}=y_{i}.y_{i}^{-i.2^{-r}} \end{equation} \noindent so as to satisfy the identity \begin{equation} c_{i}^{n-k_i}=b_{i}^{n}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Choose y_i in C near x_i with x_i=y_i y_i^{-i2^{-r}}, reducing to identity (13).
nodes.section: 3.1 Middle Third Cantor Set: An Example

nodes.name: Solve identity at endpoints
nodes.statement: To verify that (\ref{eq13}) is not empty we note that for the end points $\frac{1}{3} $ and $\frac{2}{3}$, both belonging to $C$, (\ref{eq13}) means $\left( \frac{2}{3} \right) ^{n}=$\ \ $\left( \frac{1}{3}\right) ^{n-k_1}$\ yielding $k_1=ns,$\ $s= \frac{\log 2}{\log 3}$. For this value of $k_1$, (\ref{eq13}) now tells that $ c_{i}^{1-s}=b_{i}$\ so that $c_{i}=({\frac{1}{3}})^{r}$\ and $b_{i}=\left( \frac{2}{3}\right) ^{r}$\ for a suitable $r$. Similar estimates for $k_i$ are available for other (consecutive)\ end points of (higher order) gaps.
nodes.statement_short: At endpoints 1/3, 2/3, (13) gives k_1=ns, and similar estimates hold for other gaps.
nodes.section: 3.1 Middle Third Cantor Set: An Example

nodes.name: Representation realised
nodes.statement: It thus follows that the representation (\ref{eq8}) is realised at the level of the finite Hausdorff measure of the set, when the value of the constant $k$ is real (rather than a natural number).
nodes.statement_short: The representation (8) is realised at the level of the finite Hausdorff measure.
nodes.section: 3.1 Middle Third Cantor Set: An Example

nodes.name: Gaps become infinitesimal Cantor sets
nodes.statement: Accordingly, it follows that a gap $O$ in $I/C$ ( which is a connected interval in the usual topology) containing a point $x$ of the Cantor set $C$ is indeed realised as an ``infinitesimal" Cantor set in the valuation defined by the Cantor function associated with the original Cantor set $C$ itself.
nodes.statement_short: A gap containing x is an infinitesimal Cantor set in the Cantor-function valuation.
nodes.section: 3.1 Middle Third Cantor Set: An Example

nodes.name: Outer measure
nodes.statement: It follows that $\mu _{v}$\ is a metric (Lebesgue) outer measure on $C$ realised as an ultrametric space.
nodes.statement_short: mu_v is a metric outer measure on C.

nodes.name: Diameter comparison
nodes.statement: Now for an infinitesimal (primary) scale $ \epsilon _{n}=\beta^{n}$, we can choose a sufficiently small secondary scale $ \tilde{\epsilon}_{m}=2^{-m}$, so that for any two $x$ and $y\in C$ with $ \mid x-y\mid =d$ , we have $d_{u}(x,y)$\ $=$ $\parallel x-y\parallel $ $=$ $ \tilde\epsilon _{m}^{s}\leq d^{s}\leq \left\{ d(x,y)\right\} ^{s}$, where $s=\frac{\log 2}{\log 1/\beta}$. Accordingly, it follows that $d_{u}(I_{i})\leq \left\{ \text{ }d(I_{i})\right\} ^{s}.$
nodes.statement_short: Choose secondary scale so non-archimedean diameters are at most s-th powers of Euclidean diameters.

nodes.name: Equality with H^s
nodes.statement: Using this fact and also using the monotonicity of measures one can now deduce that $\mu _{v}(E)=H^{s}(E)$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of measures gives mu_v=H^s.

nodes.name: Full set
nodes.statement: Choosing the full set $C$\ for $E$ and noting that $s$ is the Hausdorff dimension it thus follows that $\mu _{v}(C)=1.$
nodes.statement_short: Taking E=C gives mu_v(C)=1.

nodes.name: Relevance to Cantor sets
nodes.statement: The above multiplicative model of the Cauchy problem (\ref{sf}) should have a natural relevance in the context of a Cantor set (or, equivalently to an ultrametric space).
nodes.statement_short: The multiplicative model should apply on a Cantor set.

nodes.name: Lift DE to inverted Cantor set
nodes.statement: Let us now assume that the problem (\ref{sf}) is defined on a Cantor set $C$, .i.e. $x\in C$. This Cantor set is now realised as an inequivalent ultrametric space. Accordingly, each $x\in C$\ is replaced by an infinitesimal copy of the inverted Cantor set $\tilde{\bf C}$. {\em Because of scale invariance, the DE (\ref{sf}) at an $x\in C$, which is actually not defined in the usual (even in the natural ultrametric) sense, is now raised to an equation which is well defined on a closed set of the form $\tilde{\bf C}$ and treated as a multiplicative model.}
nodes.statement_short: Each x in C is replaced by an infinitesimal inverted Cantor set where the DE is well defined.

nodes.name: New solutions via LCF
nodes.statement: We note that the solution (\ref{eq21}) and (\ref{eq22}) is the standard solution derived in an unconventional way and interpreted non-trivially. On a Cantor set, however, the equation (\ref{sf}) can accommodate a host of new solutions in consonance with the multiplicative model interpretation. The origin of these new solutions could be explained in the context of locally constant functions (LCF).
nodes.statement_short: On a Cantor set the DE admits new solutions explained by locally constant functions.

nodes.name: LCF ansatz
nodes.statement: To justify, in a most natural way, the existence of locally constant functions, let us write a solution of (\ref{sf}) in the form \begin{equation} X=x \cdot x^{\tau (x^{-1})}. \end{equation} \noindent The function $\tau (x)$\ here represents a LCF and is defined by the scale free equation on logarithmic variables, viz: \bigskip \begin{equation} \log x^{-1}\frac{d\tau }{d\log x^{-1}}=\tau. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write X = x x^{tau(1/x)} with tau solving a scale free equation in log variables.

nodes.name: tau is the valuation; derivative vanishes
nodes.statement: Clearly $\tau (x)$\ corresponds to our non-trivial valuation (\ref{eq5}) denoted $v(\tilde{x})=\mid \tilde{x}$\ $\mid _{u}$. To verify $v(\tilde x)$, indeed is a LCF, we note that \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dx}v(\tilde{x})=\underset{\epsilon \rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{\log x}{\log \epsilon }+1\right) =0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Identify tau with v and check dv/dx=0.

nodes.name: Log-log variability
nodes.statement: Equation (\ref{eq26}), on the other hand, reveals the variability of a LCF over smaller logarithmic scales. Of course, the valuation also passes this test \bigskip \begin{center} $\log $ $v(\tilde{x})=\log \log \frac{x}{\epsilon }+\log \log _{\epsilon }\lambda -\log \log \epsilon ^{-1}$ \end{center} \bigskip \noindent leading to equation (\ref{eq26}) in the inverted rescaled real variable\ $ \frac{x}{\epsilon }$\ (in the $\log \log $\ scale).
nodes.statement_short: log v satisfies (26) in the log log scale.

nodes.name: Cantor function is an LCF
nodes.statement: We have already seen that $v(\tilde{x})$\ relates to an appropriate Cantor function. Consequently, a Cantor function $\phi (x)$ is shown to be a LCF with variability over $\log \log $\ scales.
nodes.statement_short: Hence a Cantor function is an LCF varying over log log scales.

nodes.name: Ultrametric extension
nodes.statement: Equation (\ref{eq25}) constitutes an ultrametric extension not only of a Cantor set, but of any connected interval of $R$ \cite{ad}. This is already verified explicitly in the $\frac{ 1}{3}$\ rd Cantor set, in Sec.3.1.
nodes.statement_short: (25) gives an ultrametric extension of Cantor sets and intervals, verified for the triadic set.

nodes.name: Summary of Example 4
nodes.statement: To summarise, we have shown that any element $x\in C_{\alpha }$\ when deformed by the non-trivial, reparametrisation invariant valuation of relative infinitesimals, is identified with an element of a 1-set $C_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Deformed elements of C_alpha are elements of a 1-set C_p.

nodes.name: Measure set by C~_p
nodes.statement: Because of this invariance, the relative infinitesimals may be assumed to live in a positive measure set $\tilde C_p$, which, in turn, determines the measure (size) of the deformed set $C_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Reparametrisation invariance lets infinitesimals live in a fat set fixing the measure of C_p.

nodes.name: Solomyak's theorem
nodes.statement: Since each element $x\in C\subset [0,1]$ is written as the arithmetic sum of two elements $ x_{0}\in C_{\alpha }$ and $x_{1}\in $\ $C_{\alpha ^{\prime }}$\ ( $C_{\alpha ^{\prime }}$ being the Cantor set of infinitesimal neighbours of $x_{0}$), it follows from a theorem of Solomyak \cite{solo} that for $\beta =\frac{1}{2}\left( 1-\alpha \right) \in \left( 0,\frac{1}{2}\right) ,$ there exists $C_{\alpha ^{\prime }}$ for a.e. $\beta ^{\prime }=\frac{1}{2}\left( 1-\alpha ^{\prime }\right) \in \left( 0,\frac{1}{2}\right) $ so that $C_{\alpha }+C_{\alpha ^{\prime }},$ has positive measure and $\frac{1}{\log \frac{1}{\beta }}+ \frac{1}{\log \frac{1}{\beta ^{\prime }}}>\frac{1}{\log 2}.$ This, therefore, constitutes an alternative proof for the said assertion. Indeed, in the above construction, the set of infinitesimals $C_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ itself is a 1-set $\tilde C_{p}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write x as a sum of points of two Cantor sets; Solomyak's theorem gives positive measure for a.e. parameter.

nodes.name: Hidden positive measure
nodes.statement: It follows, accordingly, that a slower rate of removal of middle open sets compared to a measure zero Cantor set hides a positive measure in an infinitesimal scaling factor which is exposed under the present scale invariant valuation. The uniform rate of deletion in the case of a measure zero set is violated because of the underlying reparametrisation invariance.
nodes.statement_short: Slower deletion hides a positive measure exposed by the valuation.

nodes.name: Almost sure fattening
nodes.statement: Further, in a dynamical process leading to a Cantor set, a positive measure Cantor set $C_p$ is favoured a.s (almost surely) compared to a measure zero set $C_{\alpha}$ since relative infinitesimal neighbours a.s. lie in a Cantor set $C_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ satisfying the above constraints.
nodes.statement_short: Fat Cantor sets are favoured almost surely.

nodes.name: Split the series
nodes.statement: Now, to justify the existence of such a $q$, let us first assume $\tilde u_{2m}=u^1_m$ and $\tilde u_{2m+1}= u^2_m$ such that $\sum u^i_m=l$. Then $\underset{2}{\overset {\infty}{\sum}} u_n = \sum \tilde u_{2m+1}-\sum \tilde u_{2m}=l-l=0.$ Consequently, $\alpha_{2m}=\log_{3^{(2m+1)}} (1-{\frac{3^{(2m+1)}}{2^{2m}}} u^1_m)^{-1}$ and $\alpha_{2m+1} =\log_{3^{(2m+2)}} (1+{\frac{3^{(2m+2)}}{2^{2m+1}}} u^2_m)$.
nodes.statement_short: Split u_n into even and odd parts summing to l, expressing alpha_{2m}, alpha_{2m+1}.

nodes.name: Identify LCFs
nodes.statement: Let $\eta_{2m}={\frac{3^{(2m+1)}}{2^{2m}}} u^1_m$ and $\tilde \eta_{2m+1} = {\frac{3^{(2m+2)}}{2^{2m+1}}} u^2_m$. Then the functions $(1-\eta_{2m})^{-1}$ and $1+\tilde \eta_{2m+1}$ are identified as LCF of the form eq(23) and eq(24) (Sec.4), in the neighbourhood of 1.
nodes.statement_short: The factors (1-eta)^{-1}, 1+eta are LCFs of the form (23), (24).

nodes.name: Cantor function tau
nodes.statement: Using scale invariance, we can choose for $x$ in eq(23) as $x=3^{-n}(1-\eta_{n})$ (or $x=3^{-n}(1+\tilde\eta_{n})$), and the scale factor $\epsilon=3^{-n}$. Thus, there exists a Cantor function $\tau(\tilde x), \ \tilde x=x/\epsilon$ such that $\log_{\epsilon^{-1}} \tilde x^{-1}=\tau(\tilde x) \ ( {\rm or} \ \log_{\epsilon^{-1}} \tilde x=\tau(\tilde x))$.
nodes.statement_short: By scale invariance there is a Cantor function tau with log_{1/eps} x~ = tau.

nodes.name: q^{-m_n} in the range
nodes.statement: As a result, there exists positive integers $q$ and $m_n$ so that the sequence $\{q^{-m_n}\}\subset {\rm Range} (\tau(\tilde x))$. More generally, because of the local constancy, the limiting form $\alpha_n$ could be $\alpha_n = \tilde l + q^{-m_n}$, where $\tilde l$ is a non-negative constant, $0\leq\tilde l <1$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence q^{-m_n} lies in the range of tau, possibly shifted by a constant.

nodes.name: Fattening at scale beta^n
nodes.statement: In our multiplicative representation (c.f. (\ref{eq28}) and (\ref{eq33})), the fattening size is $\epsilon=\beta^n$ and \begin{equation} x=\beta^{n}\left( \beta ^{n}\right) ^{-(l+k\beta^{n\rho}) }\times b \end{equation} \noindent where $k$ is a constant independent of $\beta$, so that the exponent $\rho$ is defined by (\ref{eq36}) when we identify $\mu(\beta^n)=\log_{\beta^{n}} (x/\beta^n)$. Notice that $\mu(0)=\underset{n\rightarrow \infty}{\lim} \log_{\beta^{n}} (x/\beta^n)=l$.
nodes.statement_short: Take epsilon=beta^n and identify mu(beta^n) with log_{beta^n}(x/beta^n), so mu(0)=l.

nodes.name: mu is the valuation
nodes.statement: Notice also that the measure $\mu$ here is nothing but the valuation of relative infinitesimals at the fattened scale $\epsilon$, which equals the full measure of the Cantor set $\tilde C_p$ at the scale $\epsilon$ (c.f. Example 4) where the infinitesimals live.
nodes.statement_short: mu is the valuation of relative infinitesimals, the measure of C~_p at scale epsilon.

nodes.name: Reparametrisation invariance
nodes.statement: Because of the reparametrisation invariance, we may suppose that $\tilde C_p$ is determined by the original 1-set and vice versa.
nodes.statement_short: C~_p and the original 1-set determine each other.

nodes.name: Fattened gaps
nodes.statement: At the scale $\epsilon$, the gaps of $\tilde C_p$ are fattened by the amount $\epsilon$, and in the presence of a positive measure, the said valuation is determined by the sum of the fattened gap sizes.
nodes.statement_short: With positive measure the valuation is the sum of fattened gap sizes.

nodes.name: Zero measure case and conclusion
nodes.statement: For a zero measure set, this valuation, on the other hand, is determined instead by the finite Hausdorff measure, upto a finer (double logarithmic) scale correction that arises from the possible presence of local fine structures (c.f., above application). This observation proves the claim.
nodes.statement_short: For null sets the valuation is set by the Hausdorff measure up to a log-log correction; this proves the claim.
